prompt: In strained.py, which data do the three command methods never read?

choices.text: holder, who has each copy and until when
choices.why: lend reads holder to refuse a copy that is out and to count a member's loans.

choices.text: titles: the names and authors
choices.why: Right. No rule needs a name; only the screens do, which is the first sign of two models in one class.

choices.text: waiting, the queue of members per title
choices.why: The reservation rule reads it: a reserved title goes to the first member in the queue.

prompt: The availability screen of strained.py visits every copy record once per title. With 40 titles and 100 copies, how many visits does one page view make?
The website wants "most borrowed this year". What happens to the single Library class?

choices.text: Nothing, because a query never changes a class
choices.why: The query needs a counter that something must keep, and the only place loans happen is lend.

choices.text: lend gains a counter that no rule reads
choices.why: Right. The rule method starts carrying screen data, which is the widening the section describes.

choices.text: The class has to be split into one class per screen before the count can be kept anywhere
choices.why: It can be kept in the one class, and usually is at first; the cost is that the class widens.

prompt: In cqs.py, why did the first shelf lend C2 instead of C1?

choices.text: The debugging line called take, which removed C1
choices.why: Right. Asking a question that is also a command performs the command.

choices.text: The list was sorted in reverse by pop
choices.why: pop(0) takes from the front and sorts nothing; C1 was simply gone already.

choices.text: print runs its arguments twice
choices.why: print evaluates each argument once; once was enough to take a copy.

prompt: Meyer's rule: a method is either a command, which changes state, or a ___, which only answers.
Two requests run if shelf.next_copy() == "C1": shelf.remove("C1") at the same moment. What is the right design?

choices.text: Keep the two calls, as the rule asks
choices.why: Both requests can see C1 free between the two calls; the rule bends exactly here.

choices.text: One atomic method that takes the copy and returns it
choices.why: Right. When answer and change must happen together, combining them is correct, as with LoadOrStore or INSERT … RETURNING.

choices.text: Call next_copy twice before removing, to be sure
choices.why: Asking twice narrows nothing; the other request can still act between the last question and the removal.

choices.text: Log every call to remove so the double loan can be undone
choices.why: A log finds the problem afterwards; the design should make it impossible.

prompt: Which of these does CQRS itself require?

choices.text: Two databases and a message bus between them
choices.why: Those are one way to place the models; the smallest version runs in one process on one file.

choices.text: Event sourcing on the write side
choices.why: Often paired with it, never required; lesson 9 is a separate decision.

choices.text: One model for commands and another for queries
choices.why: Right. Where they live and how the second is kept current are further choices.

prompt: Why is it acceptable to copy the author's name into every row of the read model?

choices.text: SQLite stores repeated text only once, so nothing is really duplicated
choices.why: It stores each row's value; the duplication is real and deliberate.

choices.text: The read model is derived, so a drift is repaired by rebuilding it
choices.why: Right. Nothing the library knows lives only there.

choices.text: Authors rarely change their names
choices.why: Rarely is not never, and titles get corrected; the copy is safe because it can be recomputed, not because it stays put.

choices.text: Normalisation is a rule for write models in Python, not for read models
choices.why: Language has nothing to do with it; the difference is between source data and derived data.

prompt: Put the three levels of separation in order, from the least to the most separated.
items: Separate code over the same tables
Separate read tables, updated in the same transaction
A separate store, updated after the write commits
trap: Staleness appears only at the third level; the second already has its own tables and is never stale.

prompt: Match each name from commands.py to what it is.

pairs.right: a command: a request that may be refused
an event: a fact that is already true
a handler: checks the rules and makes the change
the dispatch from a command's type to its handler

prompt: Dani's LendCopy is refused. What do the listeners receive?

choices.text: A CopyLent with member set to None
choices.why: No event is built at all: the refusal raises before the change and before _publish.

choices.text: Nothing
choices.why: Right. A refused command changes nothing and tells nobody.

choices.text: An event named LendRefused, so the screens can show it
choices.why: commands.py defines no such event; the refusal reaches only the caller, as an exception.

prompt: A new rule: a member with an unpaid fine cannot borrow. In the split version, where does the change go?

choices.text: Into Availability, which hides copies from that member
choices.why: A read model must never enforce a rule; it may be stale and it is not consulted by the handler.

choices.text: Into every screen that offers a Lend button
choices.why: Screens may grey out a button, and a client that skips the screen would still borrow.

choices.text: Into Lending.lend and its tests, with what it needs to know about fines
choices.why: Right. Rules live on the write side, and no screen's code is near the change.

prompt: Why does CopyLent carry was_reserved?

choices.text: So the waiting count drops without reading the queue
choices.why: Right. A read model can show only what the events say, and the queue lives on the write side.

choices.text: Because Lending uses it later to decide the next loan
choices.why: Lending has the queue itself; the field exists for readers.

choices.text: Because a frozen dataclass needs at least five fields
choices.why: A frozen dataclass can have any number of fields, including none.

choices.text: To let the projector call Lending and ask about the queue
choices.why: That call is exactly what the field avoids; a projector reading the write model rebuilds the coupling.

prompt: A third screen, "most borrowed this year", is wanted. What changes in Lending?

choices.text: A counter in lend, as in the strained class
choices.why: That was the cost before the split; now a projector counts the CopyLent events.

choices.text: A new event, BookPopular, published on every tenth loan of a title
choices.why: Popularity is a reading of loans, not a fact the rules decide; CopyLent already says everything needed.

choices.text: Nothing; a new projector counts CopyLent
choices.why: Right. A new read model is added without touching the write side.

prompt: In the last line of the read_model.py transcript, what is the waiting count for T2 after Dani borrows the copy?
In the asynchronous run of lag.py, the screen says 2 copies while both are out. Can the desk lend C2 a second time?

choices.text: Yes, because the screen is what the desk trusts when it decides to lend
choices.why: The desk may be misled, but the command goes to Lending, which knew at once.

choices.text: No: Lending refuses, because the rule reads the write model
choices.why: Right. Stale reads waste trips; they break nothing as long as no rule reads a read model.

choices.text: Only if the worker runs between the two loans
choices.why: The worker affects only the screen; the refusal does not depend on it.

choices.text: It depends on how many events are queued in the outbox
choices.why: The outbox feeds the read model and is never consulted by a handler.

prompt: Bia borrows a book and the next page does not show it. Match each remedy to how it works.

pairs.right: the screen prints what it sent, and refreshes later
the screen waits until the projection has applied the event count it was given
her own loans are updated inside the command

prompt: A search index of all loans takes seconds to update and sometimes goes down. How should it be projected?

choices.text: Asynchronously, so writes do not wait for it or fail with it
choices.why: Right. A slow or fragile read model is the case for running the projection later.

choices.text: Synchronously, so that it stays current
choices.why: Then every loan waits seconds and fails whenever the index is down.

choices.text: Neither: the handler should query the write model for searches
choices.why: That puts the screens back into the write model, the strain the lesson started from.

prompt: Which of these is the clearest case for leaving CQRS out?

choices.text: A screen that reads facts in a shape the rules never use
choices.why: That is one of the signs for it.

choices.text: A profile page that edits a record and then shows that same record
choices.why: Right. Both models would have the same shape, so the split doubles the code for nothing.

choices.text: A catalogue read thousands of times for every loan
choices.why: Reads far outnumbering writes, and scaling apart, is a reason to split.

choices.text: Several screens wanting the same loans, each in a different shape of its own
choices.why: That is Availability and MemberLoans, the case the read models were built for.

prompt: From the wc -l transcript, how many lines do commands.py and read_model.py have together?
Which of these break the lesson's rules? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A handler that checks availability by querying the read model
choices.why: Right. A rule reading a possibly stale model turns lag into a correctness bug.

choices.text: A projector that calls Lending to find out who was waiting
choices.why: Right. If a reader needs the fact, the event should carry it.

choices.text: A read model that repeats the author in every row
choices.why: That is normal: read models are derived and denormalised on purpose.

choices.text: A command that returns the id of the loan it created
choices.why: A bend the cqs section allows; returning the next screen is what it forbids.

choices.text: A method that both returns the next copy and removes it, used in a debug print
choices.why: Right. That is take from cqs.py, and the print lent a book.

prompt: Bia lends a copy in the asynchronous arrangement. Put the steps in order.
items: Lending checks the rules and records the loan
CopyLent is appended to the outbox
The worker applies CopyLent to the availability table
trap: The event is published only after the rules pass and the change is made; the read model is last.

prompt: A team adds CQRS with asynchronous projection to a small admin app whose screens each edit one record. What should they expect?

choices.text: Faster screens, since each read now comes from a table built for that one screen
choices.why: The reads were already of one record; a table per screen of the same shape buys no speed.

choices.text: More code, and edits that vanish from the screen for a moment after saving
choices.why: Right. They pay for events, projectors and the stale window, and get nothing back on screens that mirror their writes.

choices.text: No real change, since CQRS is a naming convention
choices.why: It is two models and the machinery between them; the costs are real.
